claim: Instructing a single coding agent to handle testing, architecture adherence, and edge cases simultaneously is unreliable; decomposing into independent specialized validation agents per concern works better.
stance_target: director/worker and specialized-agent decomposition over monolithic single-agent prompting
scope_conditions: production AI-agent software development practice, single practitioner case study
quoted_support: I first tried the obvious approach: detailed instructions telling the coding agent to handle testing, architecture patterns, and edge cases all at once. It never worked reliably. The breakthrough came when I loosened the constraints.

claim: An 8-gate pipeline (Requirements, Architecture, Implementation, Code Validator, Multi-Agent Code Review, CI/CD, Human Review, Deployment Verification) blocks commits at each gate until automated criteria pass, with the validator gate returning PASS/FAIL that forces re-invocation of the developer agent on failure.
stance_target: rigid, hard-blocking eval gates as the mechanism for zero-hallucination quality control in an AI software factory
scope_conditions: single practitioner's production multi-agent development pipeline
quoted_support: Commits are blocked until the validator returns PASS. If it returns FAIL, the developer agent is re-invoked to fix the issues, and the validator runs again.

claim: The Code Validator Agent rates each flagged issue on a 0-100 confidence scale requiring evidence, and only reports issues scoring 75 or above, filtering noise and false positives.
stance_target: confidence-scored, evidence-required adversarial review reduces false-positive noise in automated code review
quoted_support: Only issues with confidence >= 75 are reported. The scoring uses structured prompts that require the agent to provide evidence for each finding. No evidence, no report.

claim: Gate 5 runs four parallel specialized review agents (Architecture Compliance, Bug Detection, Security Review, E2E Test) over the full feature diff, with each flagged issue re-validated by a separate confirmation agent before being reported.
stance_target: adversarial multi-agent review architecture with cross-validation to suppress false positives
scope_conditions: Gate 5 of the described pipeline, full-feature review before PR creation
quoted_support: Four agents run simultaneously, each with a different focus: Architecture Compliance... Bug Detection... Security Review... E2E Test... Each flagged issue goes through a separate validation agent that confirms the issue actually exists.

claim: An independent code validator agent caught a converter-synchronization bug (data silently written but lost on read) that passed unit tests, type-checking, and 90%+ coverage, because the bug stemmed from a spread operator silently dropping unknown fields -- invisible to mocked tests and the type system.
stance_target: necessity of independent adversarial agent review beyond unit tests and type checking alone
scope_conditions: single real production incident at the author's company
quoted_support: The validator returned FAIL, the developer agent was re-invoked with the specific finding, and it fixed the converter in under a minute. Without Gate 4, that bug would have shipped.

claim: Persistent long-term agent memory converts one-time validator-caught failures into permanent warnings injected into future agent sessions, reducing repeat mistakes over successive runs.
stance_target: agent memory as a compounding quality-improvement mechanism, relevant to SOP/skill-sequence pillar
scope_conditions: single practitioner's agentic development workflow, described as compounding after 10+ runs
quoted_support: Gates catch problems once. Memory prevents them forever... After 10+ runs, agents start each session already knowing dozens of project-specific traps.

claim: The steady-state overhead of the full 8-gate automated quality pipeline is roughly 20 minutes per feature, independent of feature complexity, while implementation time scales with complexity.
stance_target: cost/time overhead of rigid multi-gate quality control in an agentic pipeline
quoted_support: Regardless of feature size, the validation overhead stays roughly bounded: about 20 minutes of automated checks.

claim: CI pipelines should use draft-PR gating so expensive CI runs are only triggered on code that has already passed local agent-level quality gates, conserving CI compute cost.
stance_target: cost and resource optimization pillar (avoiding wasted compute on unvalidated code)
quoted_support: PRs are always created as drafts first. CI skips draft PRs to save CI minutes... This means CI resources are only spent on code that's already passed all local gates.
